loughcrew_t.about: Cairn T (Carn Bán, the Hag's Cairn) is the central and largest passage tomb on the summit of Carnbane East (Slieve na Calliagh), the highest point in Meath, in the Loughcrew cemetery of c. 3300 BC. A cairn about 35 m across and 6-7 m high, kerbed by 37-38 slabs with the decorated 'Hag's Chair' on the north side, covers a short east-facing segmented passage (about 5 m) and a cruciform chamber: an octagonal central chamber with a corbelled beehive roof and three side cells, 28 decorated stones. Conwell cleared it in 1865 when the passage was roofless and two thirds of the chamber vault had fallen; the passage roof and chamber top were rebuilt in concrete (OPW, 1964 per the SMR; 'late 1800s' per carrowkeel.com) and a grille fills the missing keystone. Since Brennan and Roberts (1980) the equinox sunrises are known to light the decorated backstone of the rear (west) cell. The interior has been closed since 2018 for a cracked lintel.

alignment.claim: Light from the rising sun runs down the passage and forms a rectangle on the decorated backstone (C8) of the rear (west) cell, then shrinks and moves down and to the right across the motifs. The passage points 8-9° S of E, so the beam only enters when the sun is well up (about 40 minutes after sunrise); it lasts about 50 minutes and can be seen on about six days at each equinox. Its left and top edges are cut by orthostat L3 and its roofstone 5.4 m from the backstone, the bottom and right by the end-cell sill and jamb 1 m from it. Recorded on 23 March 2005; Brennan and Roberts found it in 1980.

cites.quote: Cairn T in Carnbane East is directed to receive the beams of the rising sun on the spring and autumnal equinox - the light shining down the passage and illuminating the art on the backstone.
The cairn is aligned to sunrise at the spring and autumn equinoxes and at these times people gather there to greet the first rays of the sun.

The illumination lasts for about 50 minutes and creates a striking visual effect inside the otherwise dark chamber.

knowth.about: The great mound at Knowth (Tomb 1), built and used c. 3200-2900 BC, is subcircular (95 m N-S, 80 m E-W, 10 m high) with a kerb of 127 contiguous kerbstones, most of them decorated, and covers two back-to-back passage tombs whose chambers are about 5 m apart: the eastern tomb (40.2 m long, a straight passage to a cruciform chamber with a corbelled vault 6.1 m high) and the western tomb (34.2 m, a passage bending 19-20° about 25-27 m in, to an undifferentiated chamber). Built in phases (1A dismantled; 1B the two chambers with short passages in a 38 m cairn; 1C passages lengthened to a new kerb under the great mound). In the early medieval period the mound became a rath and the passage ends were cut by ditches and souterrains, so the original entrances are lost. Excavated by George Eogan 1962-2000; the entrances were reconstructed and closed (concrete), the passages encased and propped, and the chambers are closed to visitors. The equinox alignment often claimed has been tested and rejected by Prendergast and Ray.

dowth.about: Dowth, one of the three great mounds of Brú na Bóinne (c. 3200 BC, not independently dated), is a kerbed mound about 85 m across and 15 m high with an estimated 115 kerbstones (about half visible), covering two passage tombs that open on its west side within 25 m of each other, and an early medieval souterrain. Dowth North: a passage now about 8 m long with three sills to a cruciform chamber (a large basin in the centre, pieced together in 1847) and an annex off the right recess. Dowth South: a short passage (3.3-4 m) to a circular chamber about 5 m across with one large right-hand recess; its roof is a concrete one of c. 1885-86. The 1847 excavation left a crater in the top that was never repaired. Dowth South is lit by the setting sun in the winter months, most fully around the winter solstice; Dowth North's entrance was remodelled and blocked.

carrowkeel_g.about: Cairn G is the best preserved tomb of the Carrowkeel passage tomb cemetery on the Bricklieve Mountains, Co. Sligo, at 290 m on the north end of Carrowkeel Mountain. A limestone cairn 18-21 m across and 3 m high (Macalister: 21 ft) covers a short cruciform tomb opening to the NW: a 2 m passage closed by a stone door slab, a central chamber 1.7 x 1.9 m and 2.3 m high roofed by lintels and oversailing corbels under a large flat slab, and three small cells behind high sills. Above the lintel of the entrance is a slot, the 'roof-box', through which the setting sun shines into the chamber for weeks either side of the summer solstice. Opened intact in April 1911 by Macalister, Armstrong and Praeger; burials there date to the Middle-Late Neolithic (c. 3450-2800 cal BC for the cemetery). Bog covers the base; one kerbstone is visible. Not reconstructed: the roof is original.

alignment.claim: The setting sun shines through the roof-box into the chamber for about a month (Byrne: up to six weeks) either side of the summer solstice; around the solstice it lights the back of the chamber (newgrange.com) - more exactly the left (east) recess, where it stays about two weeks: Byrne says it can never have reached the end recess. Seen from the chamber the solstice sun sets on the flat-topped Doomore; Croghaun (Ox Mountains) marks the lunar standstill. Photographed on 20 June 2008. The full moons around the winter solstice also shine in.

cites.quote: The sun enters the chamber through the roofbox at sunset for about a month before and after the summer solstice.
For the days around the summer solstice the sunset illuminates the back of the chamber.
The sun enters the chamber of Cairn G for approximately a month before and after midsummer, though it only spends about two weeks in the rear left recess of the chamber.
it is impossible that the midsummer sunset could ever have shone into the end recess of Cairn G. It currently enters the left resess of the cruciform chamber.
The sun can shine into this monument for about six weeks on either side of midsummer.
When viewed from within Cairn G, the cairn on Doomore marks the midsummer and Croghaun the lunar extreme or 'lunstice' setting positions.
The setting full moons on either side of the winter solstice also illuminate the chamber of Cairn G in much the same fashion as the sun does each summer.
Photographs of the setting sun from Cairn G on 20th June 2008.

phases.name: use of the cemetery
phases.date: c. 3450-2800 cal BC (modelled); samples 3641-2469 cal BC
phases.what: burials, cremated and unburnt; two skull fragments from Cairn G dated (Hensey et al. 2014)

cites.quote: the model supports one continuous phase of burial activity from 3454–3354 to 2894–2786 cal BC
These dates are in good agreement with two recently dated human skull fragments from Cairn G
the new study has shown that the sites were in use between c. 3,500 and 2,500 Cal. BC

phases.name: 1911 excavation
phases.what: opened intact through the entrance after removing a cover-stone; contents removed and sifted; floor flags raised

cites.quote: We began work on the morning of April 14th, with two labourers, beginning with the nearest carn ( Carn G ).
These flagstones were raised, but nothing was found underneath them.

phases.name: now
phases.what: open access, not restored; OPW preparing protective works; cairn stones lie on the chamber floor

cites.quote: they are covered with loose cairn stones at present
The Office of Public Works is preparing a program of works for the preservation and protection of Carrowkeel.

debate.claim: Where the solstice light falls: 'the back of the chamber' (newgrange.com) against the left (east) recess and never the end recess (Byrne).

cites.quote: For the days around the summer solstice the sunset illuminates the back of the chamber.
It currently enters the left resess of the cruciform chamber.

debate.claim: Lunar reading: Byrne holds that the chamber axis faces the setting extreme (major standstill) moon, not the solstice sun; unmeasured.

cites.quote: The alignment of the chamber is oriented directly the setting extreme lunar standstill.

gaps: Prendergast's thesis (Linked Landscapes, UCD 2011) and his 2018 Archaeology Ireland guide 'Solar Alignment and the Irish Passage Tomb Tradition' hold measured azimuths and horizon altitudes for Cairn T, Dowth South and Carrowkeel G; ARROW@TU Dublin (arrow.tudublin.ie) refuses scripts (Cloudflare 403), so none could be quoted. Their azimuths here are approximate.
Cairn T: Conwell's bearing E. 10° S. (1865) does not say magnetic or true; no floor-rise figure; the passage length and number of kerbstones differ between sources.

Dowth South: no azimuth, passage width or chamber height; Dowth North's original passage length is unknown (entrance rebuilt 1847-48) and its roof is called corbelled and lintelled by different sources. O'Kelly and O'Kelly 1983 (PRIA 83C, JSTOR, refuses scripts) has the measured plans.

Carrowkeel G: roof-box size and the altitude window it gives were not found; the 1911 bearing is magnetic and the conversion to true here uses an assumed variation (~20° W); cairn height 3 m (SMR) against 21 ft (Macalister) unresolved. Aaron Watson's archaeo-optic notes (aaronwatson.co.uk) refused the script.

Knowth: the SMR WEB_NOTES are cut at 8,000 characters (the end of the Tomb 1A section is lost); the Excavations at Knowth volumes (DRI repository) did not return text to the script. No floor-rise figure for the east passage beyond 'level'.
No passage-floor gradients, orthostat-by-orthostat sizes or kerbstone positions were found for any of the four (OSM maps only the outlines and the Hag's Chair).
Catalogue records: Loughcrew Q202563 and Carrowkeel Q261318 are cemetery items placed away from the tombs; Dowth's 'Dowth Mound' Q116803531 is a different mound (SMR ME020-012).
